extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic, philosophy, and scientific method (scholars, scientists, and educated readers seeking principles of evidence and inference)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria for judging inferences, the sufficiency of evidence, and the auxiliary operations (naming, definition, classification) that support scientific investigation and reasoning. Emphasis on what falls within the province of logic and how to analyze reasoning practically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of logic as science and art of reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Logic is the Science, as well as the Art, of reasoning; meaning by the former the analysis of the mental process which takes place whenever we reason, and by the latter, the rules, grounded on that analysis, for conducting the process correctly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The criterion establishes two evaluative dimensions: (1) accurate analysis/description of reasoning processes, and (2) prescriptive rules for correct conduct of those processes. Good work should both characterize how inference operates and derive usable rules from that analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logic's province: operations subservient to estimation of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Logic is the science of the operations of the understanding which are subservient to the estimation of evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate reasoning tasks by whether they address the relation between premises (data) and conclusions (what is to be proved). Material not about estimating evidence (e.g., pure introspective consciousness) falls outside logic’s remit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit logic to inferential knowledge (exclude intuition/consciousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Logic is not the science of Belief, but the science of Proof, or Evidence. With the claims which any proposition has to belief on the evidence of consciousness—that is, without evidence in the proper sense of the word—logic has nothing to do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging arguments, separate claims grounded in direct consciousness (sensations, immediate feelings) from those requiring proof. Logical evaluation focuses on inferences from premises, not on immediate intuitions themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish apparent intuition from rapid inference
rubrics_metrics.description: A truth, or supposed truth, which is really the result of a very rapid inference, may seem to be apprehended intuitively (example: perception of distance by the eye is partly a rapid inference).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critically examine whether allegedly 'intuitive' judgments are actually unconscious inferences; expose hidden premises and reasoning steps that underlie apparently immediate beliefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logic judges sufficiency of evidence but does not find evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Logic does not undertake to find evidence, but to determine whether it has been found. It neither observes, nor invents, nor discovers; but judges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should focus on whether provided data and methods suffice to establish the conclusion. The presence or absence of relevant empirical observation is for the specialist to obtain; logic evaluates the adequacy of that evidence for the intended inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include naming, definition, and classification as auxiliaries to inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Logic includes the operation of Naming; Definition, and Classification. These are operations specially instrumental to the estimation of evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess clarity and rigor of terminology, definitions, and classifications because they affect how evidence is marshaled and conclusions are drawn. Poor naming/definition is a ground for logical failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze reasoning only so far as needed to detect correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze the process of inference, and the processes subordinate to inference, so far only as may be requisite for ascertaining the difference between a correct and an incorrect performance of those processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical evaluations should not require deeper metaphysical or psychological decomposition than needed to reveal mistakes. Focus analysis on those aspects where errors in inference become visible and relevant to judging evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify relations required between data and conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Logic points out what relations must subsist between data and whatever can be concluded from them, between proof and every thing which it can prove.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing an argument, check whether the necessary relations (causal, probabilistic, analogical, deductive) between premises and conclusion are present. Identify missing conditions or unjustified transfers from facts to claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide canons/rules for testing sufficiency of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Bring together or frame a set of rules or canons for testing the sufficiency of any given evidence to prove any given proposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A rigorous review should apply explicit tests or canons (to be developed or applied) for evidence sufficiency—e.g., controls for observation, consideration of alternative causes, degree of generalization—rather than rely on intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the limits of logic relative to metaphysics and ultimate premises
rubrics_metrics.description: With the original data, or ultimate premises of our knowledge; with their number or nature, the mode in which they are obtained, or the tests by which they may be distinguished; logic, in a direct way at least, has nothing to do. These questions belong to metaphysics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not fault logical analysis for failing to settle metaphysical first principles (existence of matter, God, etc.). Evaluation should confine itself to the inferential linkages and evidence, not to resolving ultimate ontological questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize classification and taxonomy as tools for clearer evidence appraisal
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of naming, definition, and classification is to serve ... for so marshaling the facts ... as to enable us to perceive more clearly what evidence there is, and to judge with fewer chances of error whether it be sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the organization of facts and concepts improves detectability of relevant evidence and reduces confusion; poor classification that obscures relevant distinctions is a substantive fault.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and classify fallacies as a means of error detection
rubrics_metrics.description: The work contains a dedicated treatment of fallacies (classification of fallacies, fallacies of observation, fallacies of generalization, fallacies of ratiocination, etc.), i.e., common forms of incorrect reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A thorough review should screen for known fallacy types and misapplications (a priori fallacies, observational fallacies, hasty generalization, confused ratiocination) and explain which specific fallacy (if any) undermines the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of logical improvement for scientific progress
rubrics_metrics.description: In the progress of science ... each great step in advance has usually had either as its precursor, or as its accompaniment and necessary condition, a corresponding improvement in the notions and principles of logic received among the most advanced thinkers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When appraising methodological proposals or arguments, consider whether adopting clearer logical principles would materially improve their reliability or facilitate scientific progress; recommend specific logical refinements where appropriate.
